Apple today described a UK proposal targeting App Store commissions as tantamount to price control, warning it could harm innovation and investment. Details below.

Apple fights back against App Store regulation in the UK

According to Reuters, Apple today formally responded to a consultation by the UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), opposing a proposed rule that would allow app developers to link to alternative payment methods.

The CMA was able to impose such requirements after designating Apple and Google last year as holding "strategic market status" in their respective mobile platform markets. Under the UK's new digital markets regime, this designation allows the regulator to introduce company-specific rules to foster competition and give consumers more choice.

Under the proposal, Apple and Google could still charge commissions on transactions completed through alternative payment methods, but any related fees must be deemed "fair and reasonable."

Reuters noted that the CMA "expects steering fees to be lower than current App Store charges, with the savings passed on to UK consumers or reinvested in developer businesses to support innovation."

However, Apple sees things differently and has pushed back against the proposal. Here's what Reuters reported:

The CMA rejected Apple's characterisation of the proposal as price control, saying its aim is to establish principles for determining whether steering fees are fair and reasonable, rather than directly setting fee levels.
